ia.name: Historical investigation

criteria.name: Identification and evaluation of sources
look: A clear, focused question that is appropriate for a historical investigation
Two relevant sources chosen and their relevance to the question explained
Detailed analysis of the value and limitations of each source with explicit reference to origin, purpose and content

criteria.name: Investigation
look: A clearly organized, well-structured investigation that stays focused on the question
Effective use of a range of relevant sources as evidence
Critical analysis, with different perspectives considered and evaluated
A reasoned conclusion that follows from the analysis

criteria.name: Reflection
look: Reflection on what the investigation revealed about the methods historians use
Awareness of the challenges and limitations of those methods
Clear links between the reflection and the rest of the investigation

checklist: Question is narrow, answerable and phrased as a question ("To what extent…", "Why…")
Topic finished at least 10 years ago, as history rather than current affairs
Section 1 evaluates exactly two sources in depth, using their origin, purpose and content
Each evaluated source's relevance to the question is explained
Section 2 builds an argument; it is not a narrative of events
Several historians' or contemporaries' perspectives are weighed
Evidence is cited with consistent references (footnotes or in-text)
Conclusion answers the question directly and matches the argument
Section 3 reflects on historians' methods (evidence, bias, selection), linked to your investigation
Word count is within 2,200 (bibliography and footnotes excluded)
Bibliography is complete and consistently formatted

examTips: Answer the question set: underline the command term and the dates, and keep every paragraph linked back to them.
Make an argument, not a narrative: open each paragraph with an analytical claim, then support it with precise dates, names and figures.
In Paper 1 origin–purpose–content questions, explain WHY the origin or purpose makes the source valuable or limited; do not just list who wrote it.
In the Paper 1 comparison, run the links side by side ("Both A and B…, whereas…") instead of describing each source separately.
Use historiography to support your own judgement, never as a substitute for it, and finish with a conclusion that weighs the factors.
